description: I am an IT student passionate about writing and space storytelling. We are looking for a space science expert to provide accurate scientific content and 3D designers who can create realistic space environments, planets, and immersive visual scenes. We welcome creative and motivated team members who want to collaborate and bring our space stories to life through engaging and innovative visual experiences.
summary:
Footprints Beyond Earth is a bilingual (Arabic and English) interactive 3D exhibit that brings NASA's left-behind hardware back to life for kids aged 8 to 12.

Since the 1960s, NASA has left rovers, landers and probes on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each one changed what we know, yet for most kids they are just names: they don't understand their stories, or how these machines even got there.

We built a story-driven website covering 17 of these machines: 5 on the Moon, 8 on Mars and 4 in deep space. Kids pick a character, take real NASA 3D models apart part by part, and follow each machine's journey from launch to landing to discovery, such as Opportunity's proof that Mars was once wet. They can also tap planets that introduce themselves at their real positions today, and test what they learned in Play & Learn.

Every fact comes from NASA's NSSDCA archive and NASA Science mission pages, and each card cites its source. It runs on any device, with no login, connecting the engineering of each machine to the science it made possible.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Footprints Beyond Earth is a bilingual (Arabic and English) interactive 3D exhibit about 17 pieces of NASA hardware left behind: 5 on the Moon, 8 on Mars and 4 in deep space. Instead of reading a list of facts, kids aged 8 to 12 go on a guided adventure:

- Pick a character: astronaut, engineer or science detective.

- Explore real NASA 3D models part by part. Each glowing hotspot explains what that part did and why it was needed.

- Follow the story chapters, from launch to landing to discovery, for example how Opportunity found evidence that Meridiani Planum on Mars was once wet.

- Visit the Space Map, where every footprint sits on the Moon, Mars or in deep space.

- Open the Solar System, where planets sit at their real positions for today's date, spin at their true rates, and introduce themselves out loud when tapped.

- Test what they learned in Play & Learn: a short quiz and a Signal Lab showing how long a message takes to reach the Moon, Mars, Pioneer 10 or Voyager 1.

HOW IT WORKS

We used only the NASA resources listed for this challenge: the NSSDCA spacecraft catalog, experiment pages and planetary fact sheets, plus the NASA Science mission pages. Every fact is stored with the ID of the page it came from, and each story card shows its sources so teachers can check them. NASA 3D Resources models were converted and split into named, clickable parts. Planet positions are calculated from orbital elements, and anything simulated or approximate (terrain, some reconstructed models, map positions) is labelled on screen.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Kids connect the engineering of each machine to the science it made possible, instead of memorizing names.

- Teachers get a free, sourced classroom tool.

- It works on any phone or laptop, with no login, no account and no personal data, and can even run offline from a single HTML file.

- Arabic speakers get this history in their own language, with full right-to-left support.

Our goal is that these machines are no longer forgotten, and that kids see themselves as the next explorers.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber and drei, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, lucide-react, glTF-Transform and the Draco decoder, and the browser's built-in Speech Synthesis for the talking planets. Slides were designed in Canva. AI tools: Claude (coding, writing, translation and fact-checking against sources) and ElevenLabs (demo voiceover). No special hardware is needed; everything runs in the browser.

CREATIVITY

Rather than a fact sheet, each machine becomes a character with a story: kids take it apart, follow its journey, and hear the planets speak. Characters, chapters and a mission log turn learning into an adventure, while every fact stays traceable to NASA.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: facts come only from the challenge's NASA sources, and simulations are labelled.

- Age: simple language and short steps for ages 8 to 12.

- Accessibility: Arabic and English, phone-friendly layout, and a light mode for slower devices.

- Privacy and safety: no accounts, no tracking, and sound plays only when the user taps.
